opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about this question a lot, because the pull toward industry is very real, especially now. A lot of my friends from the PhD went to the big labs, and they're working with enormous compute, very talented teams, and they're seeing their work deployed to millions of people almost immediately. It would be dishonest to say I never feel tempted by that.

But looking back, I still think the decision made sense for me, and maybe it makes even more sense now than it did then. The reason is the kind of question I care about. Industry is extremely good at pushing the frontier along a direction that is already known to work: scale up, engineer better, optimize the pipeline. That's incredibly valuable, and frankly academia can't compete there. What I've always been more drawn to is the question of *why* things work, and whether there are completely different ways of doing things that nobody has seriously tried yet. Those questions often look unproductive for a long time. You might spend a year on an idea that doesn't beat any benchmark. In a company, even a very research-friendly one, it's hard to justify that for long. In academia, at least in principle, you're allowed to be wrong for a while.

Something like KANs is a good example. When we started, it was a strange idea. It wasn't obvious it would be useful, and in many ways it's still not competitive with standard architectures at scale. But it opened up a conversation about interpretability, about bringing more structure and maybe more of a scientist's mindset into neural networks. I'm not sure that kind of project would have survived the prioritization process in industry.

I also think my background in physics shapes this. Physicists have this taste for understanding: you're not satisfied when something works, you want to know the underlying principles. And I feel AI right now is a bit like physics before we had good theories. Lots of empirical phenomena, very little understanding. Someone needs to work on the understanding part, and I think academia is a natural home for that.

That said, I've become less dogmatic about it. Earlier I maybe framed it as academia versus industry, almost a matter of identity. Now I see it more as a division of labor. Industry and academia need each other. Academics should be humble about compute and scale, and use our freedom for things that are high-risk, long-term, or not obviously commercial. And if someday the most important questions I care about can only be answered with resources that only industry has, I wouldn't rule anything out. But for now, I'm happy with the choice. The freedom to follow curiosity is something I value more than I expected, and I think in the long run that's where some of the most surprising ideas come from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academia and industry generally but does not connect Liu’s decision to MIT or to a conservative academic environment.

r002.rationale: He says he has become less dogmatic, but still believes the decision made sense and is happy with it; he does not call his earlier refusal overly idealistic.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about that decision a lot, and my view of it has shifted more than once.

When I made it, it felt almost like a moral stance. I had this romantic idea that academia was where you got to ask the questions that actually mattered, where you weren't constrained by a product roadmap or a quarterly deadline. And to some degree that was true for me. I got to spend years on things like KANs, on interpretability, on these physics-inspired ways of looking at neural networks, and nobody was asking me to justify the business case. That freedom was real, and I'm grateful for it.

But I was also naive about what I was giving up. The gap between academic compute and industry compute has widened dramatically. There were moments where I had an idea I really believed in and simply couldn't test it at the scale where it would have been convincing. And meanwhile I'd watch people at the big labs run that same experiment almost as an afterthought. That's humbling. You start to wonder whether your "freedom" is really freedom if you can't actually act on it.

So now I think the framing of "academia versus industry" was itself a bit of a trap. The real question for me was always: where can I do the kind of thinking I care about, and where will that thinking have consequences? For a while, academia was clearly the better answer. Today, I'm less sure, and I've stopped treating my earlier choice as a permanent identity. It was the right decision for that period of my life. Whether it's the right decision for the next period is something I genuinely re-ask myself, and I think that's healthier than being loyal to a choice I made when I was twenty-something.

If anything, what I'd tell my younger self is: don't make it a question of virtue. Make it a question of leverage.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academia’s freedom and limits, but does not connect the choice to MIT or to a conservative academic environment.

r002.rationale: He calls his original view romantic and himself naive about what he was giving up, conveying that his refusal to enter industry was overly idealistic.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think I was too categorical about it. I treated staying in academia as a commitment to research, when those aren’t necessarily the same decision. What matters more to me now is whether I can pursue the questions I care about, with enough freedom and the right people around me. I still value academia, but I wouldn’t make staying there a goal in itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses his choice to stay in academia but does not connect it to MIT’s academically oriented, conservative environment.

r002.rationale: He calls his earlier view “too categorical,” but does not say that refusing industry was overly idealistic.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think I was a little too attached to the idea that staying in academia was the only way to do the kind of research I wanted to do. I still value the freedom to pursue fundamental questions, but I’m less convinced that the boundary between academia and industry is what matters most. The more important questions are: What can I work on? Who can I learn from? And will I have room to follow an idea that might take time to develop? So I wouldn’t dismiss my earlier determination, but I’d hold it more lightly now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses his earlier preference for academia but does not connect it to MIT or to a conservative academic environment.

r002.rationale: Calling himself “a little too attached” to the belief that academia was the only way to do his desired research conveys that he now sees his earlier refusal to enter industry as overly idealistic.
